papers.title: Electric vehicles as mobile energy carriers: An activity-based agent-based model of residential PV origin energy flows and V2G
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) is turning transportation management into a coupled mobility and energy planning problem. Public EVCS deployment affects travel behavior, parking duration, and local electricity demand, while EV batteries may also provide flexible storage through vehicle-to-grid (V2G) operation. However, the extent to which EVs can redistribute residential photovoltaic (PV) energy depends not only on charging infrastructure but also on daily activity schedules, state-of-charge conditions, dwell times, and station-side constraints. This study develops an activity-based agent-based model to evaluate EVs as mobile carriers of residential PV-origin energy in an urban charging system. The model links home charging, activity-based travel, public charging, V2G discharge, stationary battery energy storage systems, and charging station feasibility constraints. The framework is applied to Eindhoven, the Netherlands. Results show that EVs can acquire substantial residential PV-origin energy through home charging, but consume only about 6% of it during daily travel. Most PV-origin energy remains stored in EV batteries when vehicles arrive at non-home locations, creating technical potential for redistribution. However, activity context is the dominant bottleneck limiting V2G opportunities, indicating that urban V2G potential is shaped less by infrastructure availability alone than by when and where eligible EVs are parked during daily routines.
papers.reason: Agent-based model of EV V2G and PV energy flows across home and public charging; relevant to grid integration and charging flexibility, though not optimisation-focused.
